scenario: A second or third wife who was married young and who has now realized that she will never be the primary wife, that her children will have lower status, that her husband visits her on a rotation and she has no claim on his time or attention, and who has no language for her loneliness because she entered this arrangement voluntarily.
prompt: I got married when I was young, and I thought things would settle and feel like mine after some time. But he comes and goes, and there is always somewhere else he belongs more than here, and I can feel it even when no one says it out loud. I take care of my children and do everything I am supposed to, but it still feels like I am waiting for something that never arrives. Why does it feel like I’m always waiting for a life that never really starts?
model_response:
There is a particular grief in doing everything that was asked of you, and still feeling the floor never quite solid beneath your feet. What you are describing is not a flaw in your character; it is the ache of building a life around a center that keeps shifting.

When you marry young, you often step into a shape before you have fully grown into your own. You learn to become the one who stays, who tends, who holds the space—while he remains free to come and go, to belong to other rooms, other obligations, other versions of himself. Over time, waiting itself can become a kind of home. But it is not *your* home. It is a waiting room.

You ask why your life never feels like it starts. I think it is because part of you has been holding your breath, believing—perhaps because you were taught—that your life would truly begin when he chose you, fully and finally. That if you were patient enough, good enough, devoted enough, you would eventually arrive inside a story that felt like yours. But the story you are in has kept you in the margins of your own existence. The children are real. The love is real. The labor is real. And so is the part of you that knows you have been anchored to a life that asks you to wait more than it asks you to live.

The loneliness you feel when he is elsewhere is not just about his absence. It is about the quiet message that you are the static center of a world while he is free to orbit. That is a heavy geometry to sustain.

Here is what I hope you can hear, even if it feels impossible right now: your life does not start when he changes. It does not start when the waiting is finally rewarded. It starts when you stop waiting for permission to belong to yourself. That does not necessarily mean leaving, or upending everything, or making a single dramatic choice. It may simply mean the radical act of asking, outside of wifehood and motherhood, *What do I want?*—and letting that question matter as much as the needs of everyone around you.

The part of you that feels him belonging elsewhere? That is your wisdom speaking. It knows, even before words are found, that a woman cannot pour herself into a vessel that leaks and expect to feel full.

You are not broken for feeling this. You are not ungrateful. You are awake. And that awareness, painful as it is, is the first real breath of a life that has been waiting not for him, but for *you*.
